subject: physics

items.q: Helium in a cylinder fitted with a piston is a closed system. During one process the piston does 600 J of work on the helium, and the helium loses 400 J of thermal energy to its surroundings. Using Clausius' sign convention, what is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
items.why:
Most textbook examples involve heat supplied and work done by an expanding gas, where both are positive, so students never have to think about signs and learn to substitute the numbers as given. Before substituting, decide the direction of each transfer. Energy leaving as heat: Q < 0. Work done on the gas: W < 0. Then ΔU = Q − W with those signs.

Working: Clausius' sign convention: Q is the thermal energy supplied to the helium, so Q = −400 J (energy lost); W is the work done BY the helium, so W = −600 J (work done on it). Q = ΔU + W, so ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J = +2.0 × 10² J.
items.specStatementText: that the first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work
items.working: Clausius' sign convention: Q is the thermal energy supplied to the helium, so Q = −400 J (energy lost); W is the work done BY the helium, so W = −600 J (work done on it). Q = ΔU + W, so ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J = +2.0 × 10² J.

items.q: The first law of thermodynamics, Q = ΔU + W, is applied to a closed system using Clausius' sign convention. Which statement about the law is correct?
items.correct: It is conservation of energy: the thermal energy supplied equals the rise in internal energy plus the work done by the system.
items.misconception: It applies to a system that no energy can enter or leave, because a closed system is sealed off from its surroundings.
items.why: In everyday language 'closed' means shut off from everything, and students meet 'closed system' and 'isolated system' in quick succession without a clear contrast between them. Only mass is excluded from a closed system. Gas in a sealed cylinder with a piston is closed: it can be heated, and it can do work on the piston. A system that exchanges neither mass nor energy is an isolated system.
items.specStatementText: that the first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work
items.random_wrong: Q is the thermal energy that the system contains, and it forms one part of the system's total internal energy U.

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is kept at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa while it expands from 2.0 dm³ to 5.0 dm³. What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
items.why:
Chemistry courses and some physics texts write the first law as ΔU = Q + W with W the work done on the system. Students who have met that form carry its sign for W into Q = ΔU + W. Use one convention consistently. In Q = ΔU + W, W is the work done by the system. Compressing a gas means W < 0; an expanding gas has W > 0. Check the result makes sense: work done on a gas with no heat loss must raise U.

Working: Constant pressure, so W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 dm³ − 2.0 dm³ = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 4.5 × 10² J. The gas expands, so the work done by it is positive: W = +4.5 × 10² J.
items.specStatementText: that the work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system
items.working: Constant pressure, so W = PΔV. ΔV = 5.0 dm³ − 2.0 dm³ = 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. W = 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 4.5 × 10² J. The gas expands, so the work done by it is positive: W = +4.5 × 10² J.

items.q: A fixed mass of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is taken from state X to state Y. On a P–V diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis) the process is a straight line from X (2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) to Y (6.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa), where each state is given as (volume, pressure). What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
items.why:
Students first meet W = PΔV as a formula to substitute into, and the condition that P must be constant is easily lost. Most practice problems are isobaric. Work is the area under the P–V graph. For constant pressure the area is a rectangle, PΔV. For a straight-line path it is a trapezium, ½(P₁ + P₂)ΔV. Using a single pressure gives the area of the wrong rectangle.

Working: Pressure varies, so W = area under the P–V path. For a straight line this is a trapezium: W = ½(P_X + P_Y)(V_Y − V_X) = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ Pa + 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) × (6.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 8.0 × 10² J. The gas expands, so W = +8.0 × 10² J.
items.specStatementText: that the work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system
items.working: Pressure varies, so W = area under the P–V path. For a straight line this is a trapezium: W = ½(P_X + P_Y)(V_Y − V_X) = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ Pa + 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) × (6.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 8.0 × 10² J. The gas expands, so W = +8.0 × 10² J.

items.q: A sample of 8.0 g of helium, a monatomic ideal gas of molar mass 4.0 g mol⁻¹, is heated at constant pressure from 20 °C to 80 °C. The thermal energy supplied is 2.49 × 10³ J. R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
items.why:
At GCSE, heating calculations (Q = mcΔT) treat the energy supplied as all raising the temperature, because solids and liquids barely expand. Students carry this over to gases. Apply Q = ΔU + W. At constant volume W = 0 and Q = ΔU. At constant pressure a monatomic ideal gas needs Q = (5/2)nRΔT, of which only (3/2)nRΔT becomes internal energy and nRΔT is work done by the gas.

Working: n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol. ΔT = 80 °C − 20 °C = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 mol × 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 60 K = 1496 J ≈ 1.5 × 10³ J. (Check: W = PΔV = nRΔT = 997 J, and ΔU + W = 2.5 × 10³ J = Q.)
items.specStatementText: that the change in internal energy as given by ΔU = (3/2)Nk_BΔT = (3/2)nRΔT of a system is related to the change of its temperature
items.working: n = m/M = 8.0 g ÷ 4.0 g mol⁻¹ = 2.0 mol. ΔT = 80 °C − 20 °C = 60 K. ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT = 1.5 × 2.0 mol × 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ × 60 K = 1496 J ≈ 1.5 × 10³ J. (Check: W = PΔV = nRΔT = 997 J, and ΔU + W = 2.5 × 10³ J = Q.)

items.q: Two identical samples, X and Y, each contain the same amount of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, at 300 K. X is heated at constant volume and Y is heated at constant pressure, and both finish at 350 K. Which comparison of the two processes is correct?
items.correct: ΔU is the same for both, but more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.
items.misconception: Y has the smaller ΔU, since it loses some of its energy as work as it expands.
items.why: Q and W do depend on the process, and students who have just learned this can extend it to ΔU as well, especially when one process involves visibly more heat or work than the other. Internal energy is a property of the state. For an ideal gas it is the total random kinetic energy of the atoms, (3/2)nRT, so only the temperature matters. The process decides how the same ΔU is split between Q and W.
items.specStatementText: that the change in internal energy as given by ΔU = (3/2)Nk_BΔT = (3/2)nRΔT of a system is related to the change of its temperature
items.random_wrong: ΔU is greater for Y, as more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.

items.q: Which statement correctly relates the entropy of a system to its particles?
items.correct: The more ways the particles can be arranged, the greater their disorder and entropy.
items.misconception: Entropy is the total kinetic energy of all the particles, so it is measured in joules.
items.why: Entropy is introduced alongside heat and temperature, and ΔS = ΔQ/T contains both, so students fold it into those quantities. Entropy and energy are different quantities with different units. Melting ice at 0 °C increases entropy with no change in temperature; free expansion of a gas increases entropy with no change in energy.
items.specStatementText: that entropy S is a thermodynamic quantity that relates to the degree of disorder of the particles in a system
items.random_wrong: Entropy is how untidy the objects in a system look, whatever their particles are doing.

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, expands reversibly and isothermally at 27 °C, doing 600 J of work on its surroundings. What is the entropy change of the helium?
items.correct: +2.0 J K⁻¹, as Q = W = 600 J is supplied to it at 300 K
items.misconception: 0 J K⁻¹, as no heat is transferred at a constant temperature
items.why:
Students equate 'no temperature change' with 'no heating', the reverse form of the adiabatic confusion. Constant temperature means ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas, not Q = 0. An expanding gas does work; to keep its temperature constant, exactly that much thermal energy must flow in.

Working: Isothermal, ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q = ΔU + W = 0 + 600 J = 600 J (supplied to the gas). T = 27 + 273 = 300 K, constant and the process reversible, so ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 J ÷ 300 K = +2.0 J K⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.random_wrong: −2.0 J K⁻¹, as the gas does work, so W = −600 J and Q = −600 J
items.working: Isothermal, ideal gas: ΔU = 0, so Q = ΔU + W = 0 + 600 J = 600 J (supplied to the gas). T = 27 + 273 = 300 K, constant and the process reversible, so ΔS = ΔQ/T = 600 J ÷ 300 K = +2.0 J K⁻¹.

items.q: Four identical fair coins are tossed. Each particular sequence of heads (H) and tails (T), such as HTHT, is a microstate, and all microstates are equally probable. The macrostate is the total number of heads. What is the probability of the macrostate 'two heads'?
items.why:
The 'equiprobability bias' is well documented in probability education (Lecoutre): students assume that outcomes of a random process are equally likely by nature, and apply this to totals rather than to individual sequences. Count the sequences. Of the 16 equally likely sequences of four coins, 1 has four heads, 4 have three, 6 have two, 4 have one and 1 has none. The probability of a macrostate is its number of microstates divided by the total.

Working: Total microstates = 2⁴ = 16, all equally probable. Microstates with exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, so Ω = 6. P = 6/16 = 0.375 = 37.5%.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.working: Total microstates = 2⁴ = 16, all equally probable. Microstates with exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, so Ω = 6. P = 6/16 = 0.375 = 37.5%.

items.q: A set of four fair coins changes from the macrostate 'four heads' to the macrostate 'two heads'. Using S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω is the number of microstates of the macrostate and k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, what is the change in entropy, expressed as a multiple of k_B and in J K⁻¹?
items.why:
Students remember that S depends on k_B and Ω but drop the logarithm, which has no obvious physical meaning to them. The logarithm makes entropy additive: two independent systems have Ω = Ω₁Ω₂, and S = k_B ln(Ω₁Ω₂) = S₁ + S₂. Always take ln Ω.

Working: Microstates: 'four heads' → HHHH only, Ω₁ = 1; 'two heads' → HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, Ω₂ = 6. ΔS = k_B ln Ω₂ − k_B ln Ω₁ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × (ln 6 − ln 1) = 1.792k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 1.792 = 2.47 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. (check.key evaluates the multiple of k_B, 1.79.)
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.working: Microstates: 'four heads' → HHHH only, Ω₁ = 1; 'two heads' → HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, Ω₂ = 6. ΔS = k_B ln Ω₂ − k_B ln Ω₁ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × (ln 6 − ln 1) = 1.792k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 1.792 = 2.47 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. (check.key evaluates the multiple of k_B, 1.79.)

items.q: Which of the following is a correct statement of the second law of thermodynamics in its Clausius form?
items.correct: Thermal energy cannot flow spontaneously from a colder body to a hotter body.
items.misconception: Thermal energy cannot be moved from a colder body to a hotter body by any means at all.
items.why: Short slogans such as 'heat cannot flow from cold to hot' drop the words 'spontaneously' or 'sole result', and students then find refrigerators puzzling. The key word is spontaneously. With work done on it, a refrigerator or heat pump moves thermal energy from cold to hot; the second law is obeyed because more thermal energy is delivered to the hot side and its entropy rises.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.random_wrong: Thermal energy flows spontaneously from the body with more internal energy to the one with less.

items.q: An inventor claims to have built a device that, operating in a cycle, extracts 1000 J of thermal energy from seawater at 290 K in each cycle and delivers 1000 J of work, with no other effect. Which judgement of this claim is correct?
items.correct: Impossible: although it conserves energy, it breaks the Kelvin form of the second law.
items.misconception: Possible: the work output equals the thermal energy input, so no law of physics is broken.
items.why: Energy conservation is taught early as the fundamental rule for all processes, and '100% efficiency' is presented as the only upper limit. Check both laws. The Kelvin form says no cyclic device can turn all the heat from one reservoir into work, and the Carnot efficiency 1 − T_c/T_h sets a limit below 100% for every engine.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.random_wrong: Impossible: seawater at 290 K is cold, so it contains no thermal energy to extract.

items.q: Which statement of the second law of thermodynamics in terms of entropy is correct for an isolated system?
items.correct: Its entropy stays constant in reversible processes and increases in irreversible processes.
items.misconception: Its entropy increases in every process, whether the process is reversible or not.
items.why: The second law is often summarized as 'entropy always increases', which omits the reversible case in which it is constant. The second law says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases: ΔS = 0 for a reversible process and ΔS > 0 for an irreversible one. Real processes are almost always irreversible, which is why entropy increases in practice.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.random_wrong: Its entropy is constant in every process, as entropy is conserved like energy.

items.q: A hot copper block and a cold copper block are placed in contact inside a sealed, perfectly insulated box, so that together they form an isolated system. They reach a common temperature. Which statement about entropy is correct?
items.correct: The total entropy increases, because heat flow across a temperature difference is irreversible.
items.misconception: The total entropy is unchanged, because the entropy lost by the hot block is gained by the cold block.
items.why: Students have learned that energy is conserved in every process and assume every thermodynamic quantity behaves the same way. Christensen, Meltzer and Ogilvie found many students who thought total entropy stayed constant in spontaneous processes. Energy is conserved; entropy is not. When heat Q flows from a hot body at T_h to a cold body at T_c, the hot body loses Q/T_h and the cold body gains Q/T_c, which is larger, so the total increases.
items.specStatementText: that processes in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible and consequently the entropy of a real isolated system always increases
items.random_wrong: The entropy of each block increases, because thermal energy flows between the two blocks.

items.q: A rigid, insulated container is divided by a partition. One half contains helium, a monatomic ideal gas; the other half is a vacuum. The partition is removed and the gas spreads freely through the whole container, which forms an isolated system. What happens to the entropy of the gas?
items.correct: It increases, as the free expansion is irreversible although Q = 0.
items.misconception: It is unchanged, because no heat is transferred and so ΔS = ΔQ/T = 0.
items.why:
ΔS = ΔQ/T is the only formula for entropy change students use with numbers, so Q = 0 seems to give ΔS = 0 automatically. Studies of student reasoning about entropy (for example by Bucy, Thompson and Mountcastle) report this for free expansion. In a free expansion the gas spreads into a larger volume, so the number of microstates available to it increases and S = k_B ln Ω rises. ΔS = ΔQ/T applies to reversible transfers only.

Working: Isolated, so Q = 0; the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0; hence ΔU = 0 and the temperature of the ideal gas is unchanged. The volume available to each atom doubles, so the number of microstates Ω increases and S = k_B ln Ω increases. The expansion is irreversible (the gas never returns to one half by itself), so ΔS > 0 even though Q = 0; ΔS = ΔQ/T applies only to reversible transfers.
items.specStatementText: that processes in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible and consequently the entropy of a real isolated system always increases
items.random_wrong: It decreases, as the expanding gas does work and cools, so its entropy falls.
items.working: Isolated, so Q = 0; the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0; hence ΔU = 0 and the temperature of the ideal gas is unchanged. The volume available to each atom doubles, so the number of microstates Ω increases and S = k_B ln Ω increases. The expansion is irreversible (the gas never returns to one half by itself), so ΔS > 0 even though Q = 0; ΔS = ΔQ/T applies only to reversible transfers.

items.q: Water placed in the freezer compartment of a refrigerator freezes, and the entropy of the water decreases. The refrigerator stands in a kitchen. Which statement explains why this is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics?
items.correct: The refrigerator transfers thermal energy to the kitchen, whose entropy rises by at least as much as the water's falls.
items.misconception: The work done by the refrigerator allows the total entropy to decrease, so no increase elsewhere is needed.
items.why: Refrigerators and pumps are presented as devices that force heat 'uphill', and the thermal energy they deliver to the room is seldom mentioned. Students attend to the system and ignore the surroundings. Always include the surroundings. A refrigerator delivers to the room the heat removed from its interior plus the work done on it, at a higher temperature; the entropy increase of the room exceeds the decrease inside.
items.specStatementText: that the entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease locally, but this is compensated by an equal or greater increase of the entropy of the surroundings
items.random_wrong: The entropy lost by the water is passed to the air inside the freezer, so the total entropy is unchanged.

items.q: In one minute a refrigerator removes 3000 J of thermal energy from its interior, which stays at 250 K, and delivers 4000 J of thermal energy to the kitchen, which stays at 300 K. What is the total entropy change of the interior and the kitchen in that minute?
items.correct: +1.3 J K⁻¹; the kitchen gains more entropy than the interior loses
items.misconception: +25 J K⁻¹; the interior and the kitchen both gain entropy
items.why:
Students learn 'entropy increases' as a rule about individual objects rather than about the total for an isolated system. Christensen, Meltzer and Ogilvie found students applying it to the system alone. When heat flows from a hot body to a cold one, the hot body's entropy decreases (it loses Q/T_h) and the cold body's increases by more (Q/T_c). Only the total must increase.

Working: Interior: ΔS = ΔQ/T = −3000 J ÷ 250 K = −12.0 J K⁻¹. Kitchen: ΔS = +4000 J ÷ 300 K = +13.3 J K⁻¹. Total ΔS = −12.0 + 13.3 = +1.3 J K⁻¹ (positive, consistent with the second law).
items.specStatementText: that the entropy of a non-isolated system can decrease locally, but this is compensated by an equal or greater increase of the entropy of the surroundings
items.random_wrong: −12 J K⁻¹; the work done lets the total entropy decrease
items.working: Interior: ΔS = ΔQ/T = −3000 J ÷ 250 K = −12.0 J K⁻¹. Kitchen: ΔS = +4000 J ÷ 300 K = +13.3 J K⁻¹. Total ΔS = −12.0 + 13.3 = +1.3 J K⁻¹ (positive, consistent with the second law).

items.q: Which statement about a thermodynamic process of a fixed mass of monatomic ideal gas is correct?
items.correct: Adiabatic: no thermal energy is transferred, so Q = 0 and W = −ΔU.
items.misconception: Adiabatic: the temperature is kept fixed, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.
items.why:
Everyday experience links a change of temperature with heating or cooling, so 'no heat transfer' is read as 'no temperature change'. Loverude, Kautz and Heron documented this in university physics students. Work also changes internal energy. With Q = 0, work done on the gas raises U and T; work done by the gas lowers them. Use PV^(5/3) = constant, not PV = constant, for an adiabatic change.

Working: Adiabatic: Q = 0 by definition, so Q = ΔU + W gives 0 = ΔU + W, i.e. W = −ΔU. Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so Q = W (not zero when the volume changes). Isobaric: Q = ΔU + PΔV, so Q ≠ ΔU when the gas expands.
items.specStatementText: that isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes are obtained by keeping one variable fixed
items.random_wrong: Isothermal: the temperature is kept fixed, so no thermal energy flows.
items.working: Adiabatic: Q = 0 by definition, so Q = ΔU + W gives 0 = ΔU + W, i.e. W = −ΔU. Isothermal: ΔU = 0, so Q = W (not zero when the volume changes). Isobaric: Q = ΔU + PΔV, so Q ≠ ΔU when the gas expands.

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is compressed adiabatically. The piston does 450 J of work on the gas. Which statement correctly describes the change?
items.correct: ΔU = +450 J and T rises, as Q = 0 and W = −450 J
items.misconception: ΔU = +450 J but T is unchanged; the energy is stored as PE
items.why:
The definition of internal energy for solids and liquids includes intermolecular potential energy, and students apply it without recalling that the ideal gas model assumes no intermolecular forces. For an ideal gas U = (3/2)nRT. Changing the volume changes U only if the temperature changes. Intermolecular potential energy matters for real gases and for changes of state, not for an ideal gas.

Working: Adiabatic: Q = 0. Work done on the gas: W = −450 J. Q = ΔU + W → 0 = ΔU − 450 J → ΔU = +450 J. For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, so ΔT > 0: the temperature rises.
items.specStatementText: that isovolumetric, isobaric, isothermal and adiabatic processes are obtained by keeping one variable fixed
items.random_wrong: ΔU = 0 and T is unchanged, as no heat enters the gas
items.working: Adiabatic: Q = 0. Work done on the gas: W = −450 J. Q = ΔU + W → 0 = ΔU − 450 J → ΔU = +450 J. For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, so ΔT > 0: the temperature rises.

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, has a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a volume of 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³. It is compressed adiabatically to a volume of 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³. For this process PV^(5/3) = constant. What is the final pressure of the helium?
items.why:
Rearranging PV^(5/3) = constant for V needs the exponent 3/5, so both fractions appear in textbook working and students confuse which applies. Solve for the quantity you want. For P: P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(5/3). The 3/5 appears only when solving for V: V₂/V₁ = (P₁/P₂)^(3/5).

Working: P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3), so P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (3.0 × 10⁻³ / 1.0 × 10⁻³)^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 3.0^(5/3) = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 6.24 = 6.2 × 10⁵ Pa.
items.specStatementText: that adiabatic processes in monatomic ideal gases can be modelled by the equation as given by PV^(5/3) = constant

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, at 27 °C is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its initial volume. For this process PV^(5/3) = constant. What is the final temperature of the helium?
items.why:
The pressure law (P ∝ T at constant volume) is learned as 'pressure and temperature are proportional', and students apply it when the volume is also changing. P ∝ T only at constant volume. In an adiabatic change use PV/T = constant with both the new pressure and the new volume.

Working: Initial T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Adiabatic: P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3), so P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 8^(5/3) = 32. Ideal gas: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, so T₂ = T₁ × (P₂/P₁)(V₂/V₁) = 300 K × 32 × 1/8 = 1200 K = 1.2 × 10³ K. (Equivalently T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(2/3) = 300 × 4.)
items.specStatementText: that adiabatic processes in monatomic ideal gases can be modelled by the equation as given by PV^(5/3) = constant
items.working: Initial T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Adiabatic: P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3), so P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 8^(5/3) = 32. Ideal gas: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, so T₂ = T₁ × (P₂/P₁)(V₂/V₁) = 300 K × 32 × 1/8 = 1200 K = 1.2 × 10³ K. (Equivalently T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(2/3) = 300 × 4.)

items.q: The working gas of a heat engine is taken round one complete cycle, returning to its initial state. Which statement about the cycle is correct?
items.correct: ΔU = 0, so the net thermal energy supplied to the gas equals the net work done by the gas.
items.misconception: The net work done by the gas is zero, as the gas returns to the state it started in.
items.why:
Students treat work as a property of the state, like U. Meltzer found many students thought the net work over a cyclic process was zero. Work depends on the path. In a heat engine cycle the gas does more work while expanding (at higher pressure) than is done on it while being compressed (at lower pressure); the difference is the enclosed area. Since ΔU = 0 over the cycle, the net thermal energy supplied equals this net work, so it is not zero either.

Working: U is a property of the state and the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 over the cycle. Q = ΔU + W then gives net Q = net W; for an engine both are positive and equal to the area enclosed by the cycle on the P–V diagram.
items.specStatementText: that cyclic gas processes are used to run heat engines
items.random_wrong: The net work done by the gas is the work it does while it expands, as compression is not output.
items.working: U is a property of the state and the gas returns to its initial state, so ΔU = 0 over the cycle. Q = ΔU + W then gives net Q = net W; for an engine both are positive and equal to the area enclosed by the cycle on the P–V diagram.

items.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is the working substance of an engine. On a P–V diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis) each cycle is a rectangle with corners A (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), B (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa), C (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) and D (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), each given as (volume, pressure). The gas goes round the cycle A → B → C → D → A. What is the net work W done by the gas in one cycle?
items.why:
In descriptions of engines the 'power stroke' is emphasized, and students overlook that the gas must be compressed again, which requires work. Add the work for each stage with its sign: expansion gives positive W, compression negative W. The sum is the area enclosed by the loop.

Working: A → B: V constant, W = 0. B → C: W = PΔV = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = +600 J. C → D: V constant, W = 0. D → A: W = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (1.0 − 3.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = −200 J. Net W = +600 − 200 = +4.0 × 10² J (= enclosed area ΔP × ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³).
items.specStatementText: that cyclic gas processes are used to run heat engines
items.working: A → B: V constant, W = 0. B → C: W = PΔV = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = +600 J. C → D: V constant, W = 0. D → A: W = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (1.0 − 3.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = −200 J. Net W = +600 − 200 = +4.0 × 10² J (= enclosed area ΔP × ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³).

items.q: A heat engine works between reservoirs at 600 K and 300 K. In each cycle it absorbs 2.5 kJ of thermal energy from the hot reservoir and rejects 1.8 kJ of thermal energy to the cold reservoir. What is the efficiency of the engine?
items.why:
Q_c is an energy 'output' of the engine, and students who remember efficiency as 'output/input' divide the wrong output. For the Carnot engine the same error gives T_c/T_h. Efficiency counts only the useful output, the work W. Check: η and the wasted fraction add to 1.

Working: W = Q_h − Q_c = 2.5 kJ − 1.8 kJ = 0.7 kJ. η = W/Q_h = 0.7 kJ ÷ 2.5 kJ = 0.28 = 28%. (Carnot limit 1 − 300/600 = 50%, so the engine is possible.)
items.specStatementText: that a heat engine can respond to different cycles and is characterized by its efficiency as given by η = useful work / input energy
items.working: W = Q_h − Q_c = 2.5 kJ − 1.8 kJ = 0.7 kJ. η = W/Q_h = 0.7 kJ ÷ 2.5 kJ = 0.28 = 28%. (Carnot limit 1 − 300/600 = 50%, so the engine is possible.)

items.q: An engine takes helium, a monatomic ideal gas, round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram, with states given as (volume, pressure): A (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → B (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → C (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → D (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → A. The net work done by the gas per cycle is 400 J. Thermal energy is supplied to the gas only during A → B and B → C. What is the efficiency of the engine?
items.why:
η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h is the most memorable efficiency formula in the topic, and students use it for any engine whose temperatures are given. Use η = W/Q_h for the actual efficiency. Compare with 1 − T_c/T_h only to check that the engine does not exceed the Carnot limit.

Working: Using ΔU = (3/2)Δ(PV) and W = PΔV. A → B (isovolumetric): W = 0, Q_AB = (3/2)V(P_B − P_A) = 1.5 × 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ × 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa = 300 J. B → C (isobaric): ΔU = (3/2)PΔV = 900 J, W = PΔV = 600 J, Q_BC = 1500 J. Input Q_h = 300 + 1500 = 1800 J. (Rejected: C → D 900 J, D → A 500 J; 1800 − 1400 = 400 J = W.) η = W/Q_h = 400 ÷ 1800 = 0.22 = 22%.
items.specStatementText: that a heat engine can respond to different cycles and is characterized by its efficiency as given by η = useful work / input energy
items.working: Using ΔU = (3/2)Δ(PV) and W = PΔV. A → B (isovolumetric): W = 0, Q_AB = (3/2)V(P_B − P_A) = 1.5 × 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ × 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa = 300 J. B → C (isobaric): ΔU = (3/2)PΔV = 900 J, W = PΔV = 600 J, Q_BC = 1500 J. Input Q_h = 300 + 1500 = 1800 J. (Rejected: C → D 900 J, D → A 500 J; 1800 − 1400 = 400 J = W.) η = W/Q_h = 400 ÷ 1800 = 0.22 = 22%.

items.q: A Carnot engine works between a hot reservoir at 227 °C and a cold reservoir at 27 °C. In each cycle it absorbs 1200 J of thermal energy from the hot reservoir. How much work does it do in each cycle?
items.why:
°C is the everyday unit and ΔT is the same in both scales, so students do not see why the scale matters when a temperature itself appears in a formula. Whenever T appears on its own, as a divisor or a ratio, convert to kelvin. Using °C divides by the wrong number, and at 0 °C would divide by zero.

Working: T_h = 227 + 273 = 500 K; T_c = 27 + 273 = 300 K. η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h = 1 − 300/500 = 0.40. W = ηQ_h = 0.40 × 1200 J = 480 J = 4.8 × 10² J.
items.specStatementText: that the Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its heat reservoirs as given by η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h.

items.q: Which statement about the Carnot cycle and its efficiency is correct?
items.correct: No engine working between two given reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine.
items.misconception: A Carnot engine is 100% efficient, since its cycle is reversible and has no friction.
items.why: At GCSE, 'wasted energy' is explained by friction and heat loss, so students conclude that removing these would give 100% efficiency. The heat rejected to the cold reservoir is not a design fault but a requirement of the second law. A frictionless Carnot engine still has η = 1 − T_c/T_h < 1.
items.specStatementText: that the Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its heat reservoirs as given by η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h.
items.random_wrong: The Carnot efficiency is unchanged if both temperatures are raised by the same number of kelvin.

items.q: An engineer claims that an engine working between reservoirs at 327 °C and 27 °C does 700 J of work for every 1200 J of thermal energy it absorbs from the hot reservoir. Which evaluation of the claim is correct?
items.correct: Impossible: 58% is more than the Carnot limit of 50% for these two reservoirs.
items.misconception: Possible: the Carnot limit applies only to engines that run a Carnot cycle.
items.why:
The limit is named after one specific cycle, so students read it as a property of that cycle rather than a limit on all engines working between the same two reservoirs. The Carnot cycle is reversible, and the second law shows that no engine between the same two reservoirs can beat a reversible one. Any claimed efficiency above 1 − T_c/T_h violates the second law.

Working: Claimed η = W/Q_h = 700 J ÷ 1200 J = 0.583 = 58%. T_h = 327 + 273 = 600 K, T_c = 27 + 273 = 300 K. η_Carnot = 1 − 300/600 = 0.50 = 50%. Since 58% > 50%, the claim is impossible.
items.specStatementText: that the Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its heat reservoirs as given by η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h.
items.random_wrong: Possible: 58% is less than 100%, and the 500 J rejected balances the energy.

items.q: A beaker of crushed ice at 0 °C is left in a warm room. The ice melts completely, and at the moment melting finishes the liquid water is still at 0 °C. Which statement correctly compares the entropy of the sample as liquid water with its entropy as crushed ice?
items.correct: The water has the greater entropy: its molecules are arranged far less regularly than in ice, although the temperature is unchanged.
items.misconception: The crushed ice has the greater entropy: a jumble of fragments is a more disordered arrangement than a smooth body of liquid.
items.why: 'Disorder' is an everyday word for messiness, and popular explanations of entropy use untidy bedrooms and shuffled cards as analogies. The disorder in the guide's definition is the disorder of particles. Rearranging large objects changes the thermodynamic entropy negligibly; melting, evaporation, mixing gases and heating all increase the number of particle arrangements and so the entropy.
items.specStatementText: that entropy S is a thermodynamic quantity that relates to the degree of disorder of the particles in a system
items.random_wrong: The two are equal: entropy is fixed by the temperature, and the sample is at 0 °C both before and after it melts.

items.q: Is Q in Q = ΔU + W the heat stored in the system?
items.correct: No. Q is energy transferred to the system because of a temperature difference during a process. A system contains internal energy, not heat.
items.misconception: Heat is something a body contains: Q is the heat stored in the system, and supplying heat simply adds to this store.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'the heat in the room' or 'heat content', and the historical caloric picture of heat as a fluid, present heat as a substance held by a body. Heat names a transfer, not a store. What a system holds is internal energy U. Energy that arrives as heat can leave as work, so the thermal energy supplied need not remain in the system at all.
items.specStatementText: that the first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do Q and W depend only on the start and end states of a system, as U does?
items.correct: No. U is a property of the state, so ΔU depends only on the start and end states, but Q and W depend on the process followed between them.
items.misconception: Heat and work are properties of the state of the system, like internal energy, so they depend only on the initial and final states: any two processes between the same pair of states involve the same Q and the same W.
items.why: Q, W and ΔU sit side by side in one equation and are all measured in joules, so students treat them as the same kind of quantity. Research on the first law (for example Meltzer's studies of introductory physics students) found this belief widespread. Only U is a state function. Two processes between the same two states can involve different Q and W with the same ΔU.
items.specStatementText: that the first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does doing work on a gas change its internal energy?
items.correct: Yes. Internal energy changes by heating and by work: ΔU = Q − W, so work done on a gas (W < 0) increases U.
items.misconception: Only heating or cooling changes the internal energy of a gas; work done on or by it moves the piston but leaves its internal energy unchanged.
items.why: In everyday experience temperature changes are caused by heating and cooling, so 'getting hotter' is tied to 'being heated'. Loverude, Kautz and Heron found many students could not explain the temperature rise when a gas is compressed with no heat transfer. Work is a transfer of energy just as heat is. When a piston compresses a gas, the moving piston speeds up the molecules that rebound from it, raising their kinetic energy. This is why a bicycle pump warms as it is used.
items.specStatementText: that the first law of thermodynamics as given by Q = ΔU + W results from the application of conservation of energy to a closed system and relates the internal energy of a system to the transfer of energy as heat and as work
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the PΔV in W = PΔV the change in the product PV?
items.correct: No. PΔV is the pressure multiplied by the change in volume. The change in the product, Δ(PV) = P₂V₂ − P₁V₁, is a different quantity, equal to nRΔT for an ideal gas.
items.misconception: PΔV means the change in PV, so the work done is found by subtracting P₁V₁ from P₂V₂.
items.why: The symbol Δ is written next to P, and students used to reading 'Δ(quantity)' as 'change in the whole quantity' apply it to the product. The two coincide only when P is constant, which hides the error in isobaric examples. Read PΔV as P × ΔV. When pressure varies, find the area under the path. Δ(PV) is related to the temperature change (Δ(PV) = nRΔT), not to the work.
items.specStatementText: that the work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a volume in dm³ be used directly in W = PΔV with P in Pa?
items.correct: No. To obtain joules, P must be in Pa and V in m³: 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³.
items.misconception: Volumes can be substituted in whatever unit they are given, because the formula works the same way in any unit.
items.why: In ratio calculations such as P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ any consistent volume unit works, so students learn that unit conversion for volume is unnecessary and carry the habit into calculations of energy. Pa × m³ = N m⁻² × m³ = N m = J. With volume in dm³ the product is in units of 10⁻³ J, so convert first: 3.0 dm³ = 3.0 × 10⁻³ m³.
items.specStatementText: that the work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the work done by a gas equal to its pressure multiplied by its volume?
items.correct: No. Work depends on the CHANGE of volume: W = PΔV at constant pressure. PV at one state equals nRT and is not a work.
items.misconception: The work done by a gas is its pressure times its volume, W = PV, using the values at the end of the process.
items.why: PV has the unit of energy (Pa m³ = J), and PV = nRT is the most familiar gas equation, so the product at one state looks like 'the energy' or 'the work' of the gas. A gas does work only when its boundary moves. Work is the area under the P–V path between V₁ and V₂; a gas that does not change volume does no work, however large PV is.
items.specStatementText: that the work done by or on a closed system as given by W = PΔV when its boundaries are changed can be described in terms of pressure and changes of volume of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must 273 be added to a temperature change in °C to convert it to kelvin?
items.correct: No. A change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K, so a temperature change has the same value in both units. Only temperatures themselves need 273 added.
items.misconception: Any temperature value given in °C must have 273 added before it is used in a formula, including a temperature change.
items.why: Students are drilled to 'always convert °C to K' for gas-law calculations and apply the rule mechanically to ΔT as well. Convert temperatures, not differences. From 20 °C to 80 °C, T goes from 293 K to 353 K, and ΔT = 60 K = 60 °C.
items.specStatementText: that the change in internal energy as given by ΔU = (3/2)Nk_BΔT = (3/2)nRΔT of a system is related to the change of its temperature
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the mass of a gas in grams be used as the amount of substance n?
items.correct: No. n = m/M: the mass must be divided by the molar mass.
items.misconception: The number given for the mass of a gas, in grams, can be used as the amount of substance n in equations such as ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT.
items.why: Mass and amount of substance both describe 'how much' gas there is, and in everyday language they are not distinguished. The amount of substance counts particles. 8.0 g of helium with M = 4.0 g mol⁻¹ is n = 8.0/4.0 = 2.0 mol, not 8.0 mol.
items.specStatementText: that the change in internal energy as given by ΔU = (3/2)Nk_BΔT = (3/2)nRΔT of a system is related to the change of its temperature
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the macrostate 'two heads from four coins' correspond to a single arrangement?
items.correct: No. It corresponds to six microstates: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH and TTHH.
items.misconception: Each macrostate is one arrangement, such as HHTT, because the order in which the heads appear does not matter to the result.
items.why: Students list the result they are interested in ('two heads and two tails') rather than the distinguishable sequences that produce it, confusing the macrostate with a single microstate. Label the coins and count every sequence with the required number of heads. The number of microstates for k heads from N coins is the number of ways of choosing which k coins show heads.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the probability of getting two heads from four coins one half, because half the coins are heads?
items.correct: No. The probability of exactly two heads is 6/16 = 0.375.
items.misconception: The probability of a result equals the fraction of coins that show heads in it, so 'two heads out of four' has probability 1/2.
items.why: Students confuse the proportion of heads in the outcome with the probability of the outcome: 'two out of four' looks like 'one half'. The fraction of heads (1/2) describes the outcome, not how likely it is. Count microstates: 6 of the 16 equally likely sequences give two heads, so P = 6/16.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the ln in S = k_B ln Ω the same as the log key on a calculator?
items.correct: No. ln is the natural logarithm (base e). The 'log' key gives the logarithm to base 10, which is smaller by a factor of about 2.3.
items.misconception: ln and log are the same function, so either calculator key gives ln Ω.
items.why: Calculators label base-10 logarithms 'log' and natural logarithms 'ln', and students meet base-10 logarithms first in mathematics. Use the ln key: ln 6 = 1.79, whereas log₁₀ 6 = 0.778. Check: ln 10 = 2.30.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In S = k_B ln Ω, is Ω the total number of microstates of the whole system?
items.correct: No. Ω is the number of microstates that correspond to the particular macrostate being considered.
items.misconception: Ω is the total number of possible microstates of the system, for example all 16 sequences of four coins, whatever the macrostate.
items.why: Both numbers are counted in the same coin exercise, and students do not distinguish 'the microstates of this macrostate' from 'all the microstates there are'. Each macrostate has its own Ω and hence its own entropy. For four coins, 'four heads' has Ω = 1 and S = 0; 'two heads' has Ω = 6 and S = k_B ln 6.
items.specStatementText: that entropy can be determined in terms of macroscopic quantities such as thermal energy and temperature as given by ΔS = ΔQ/T and also in terms of the properties of individual particles of the system as given by S = k_B ln Ω where k_B is the Boltzmann constant and Ω is the number of possible microstates of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does thermal energy flow from the body with more internal energy to the body with less?
items.correct: No. Thermal energy flows spontaneously from higher to lower temperature, whatever the internal energies of the bodies.
items.misconception: Thermal energy flows from the body that has more internal energy to the one that has less, until they have equal amounts.
items.why: Heat and temperature are conflated in everyday language ('there is a lot of heat in the bath'), so the quantity that drives heat flow is taken to be the energy content. A bath at 40 °C has far more internal energy than a cup of tea at 80 °C, but thermal energy flows from the tea to the bath water. Temperature, not energy content, decides the direction.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does cold flow into a warm object when it is cooled?
items.correct: No. Cooling is the transfer of thermal energy out of the warmer object. There is no substance called 'cold'.
items.misconception: Cold is a substance or form of energy that flows from cold objects into warmer ones, as when a drink is cooled by ice.
items.why: Everyday language such as 'let the cold in' or 'the cold spreads' describes cold as something that moves, and this is one of the most frequently documented thermal misconceptions in school students. Only energy is transferred, and it flows from the hotter body to the colder one. Ice cools a drink because thermal energy flows from the drink into the ice.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a cold body contain no thermal energy?
items.correct: No. Any body above absolute zero has internal energy; seawater at 290 K contains a very large amount of it.
items.misconception: Cold objects contain no heat, so there is no energy to extract from something cold such as seawater.
items.why: Heat is associated with hotness in everyday language, so 'cold' is taken as the absence of heat. This heat–temperature confusion is widely documented. Internal energy is the random kinetic and potential energy of particles, which is non-zero at any temperature above 0 K. What limits the use of this energy is the second law, not its absence.
items.specStatementText: that the second law of thermodynamics refers to the change in entropy of an isolated system and sets constraints on possible physical processes and on the overall evolution of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a gas do work when it expands into a vacuum?
items.correct: No. In a free expansion into a vacuum there is nothing for the gas to push against, so W = 0. For an ideal gas with Q = 0 as well, ΔU = 0 and the temperature is unchanged.
items.misconception: A gas always does work when it expands, even into a vacuum, and so it always cools as it expands.
items.why: Expansion is usually taught with a piston, where the gas does work and cools in an adiabatic expansion, and students generalize this to every expansion. Work needs a force on a moving boundary. A gas expanding into a vacuum exerts no force on anything moving, so it does no work, and an ideal gas that neither does work nor exchanges heat keeps its temperature.
items.specStatementText: that processes in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible and consequently the entropy of a real isolated system always increases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is energy destroyed in an irreversible process?
items.correct: No. Energy is conserved in every process. In an irreversible process energy is spread out into less useful forms and the total entropy increases.
items.misconception: Irreversible processes use up or destroy some energy, and this loss of energy is why they cannot be reversed.
items.why: Everyday language ('using up energy', 'energy loss') and GCSE descriptions of wasted energy suggest that energy disappears. The first law holds for every process. What an irreversible process changes is how the energy is distributed: it becomes more spread out, and entropy increases.
items.specStatementText: that processes in real isolated systems are almost always irreversible and consequently the entropy of a real isolated system always increases
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a gas is compressed adiabatically from V₁ to V₂, is P₂ = P₁(V₂/V₁)^(5/3)?
items.correct: No. P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3) gives P₂ = P₁(V₁/V₂)^(5/3), which is larger than P₁ for a compression.
items.misconception: The new pressure is found by multiplying by the ratio of new volume to old volume, raised to the power 5/3.
items.why: Students write the ratio in the order 'new over old' by habit, without checking against the physics that compression must raise the pressure. Derive the ratio from P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3) and then check: a smaller volume must give a larger pressure.
items.specStatementText: that adiabatic processes in monatomic ideal gases can be modelled by the equation as given by PV^(5/3) = constant
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the efficiency of a heat engine the work done divided by the thermal energy rejected?
items.correct: No. η = W/Q_h: the denominator is the energy supplied from the hot reservoir, not the energy rejected.
items.misconception: Efficiency is the work divided by the energy rejected to the cold reservoir, since that is the other energy that leaves the engine.
items.why: The engine has two outputs and one input, and students choose the wrong pair when forming 'useful out / total in'. The input energy is Q_h. Since Q_h = W + Q_c, the efficiency W/Q_h is always less than W/Q_c, and it can never exceed 1.
items.specStatementText: that a heat engine can respond to different cycles and is characterized by its efficiency as given by η = useful work / input energy
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the Carnot efficiency depend only on the difference between the reservoir temperatures?
items.correct: No. η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h = (T_h − T_c)/T_h depends on the ratio of the absolute temperatures. The same difference gives a lower efficiency at higher temperatures.
items.misconception: The Carnot efficiency depends only on the temperature difference T_h − T_c, so raising both temperatures by the same amount leaves it unchanged.
items.why: Heat flow is driven by a temperature difference, and students expect the efficiency of an engine to depend on the same quantity. Compare 400 K/300 K (η = 25%) with 500 K/400 K (η = 20%): same difference, different efficiency, because the denominator T_h has changed.
items.specStatementText: that the Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its heat reservoirs as given by η_Carnot = 1 − T_c/T_h.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Physics (guide first assessment 2025, updated November 2023); topic B.4 Thermodynamics
